warmup.q: Half of the report step's calls finish within 1.5 µs, but the slowest one in ten thousand (the p99.99) takes 36.7 ms. The program ran 14 garbage collections in 3 seconds. Where do you look first?
options: The document store, since slow calls usually wait for the network
Allocation: the rare slow calls most likely waited for GC pauses, and the GC runs often because the code allocates a lot
The JIT: 36.7 ms is a compilation
warmup.why: Most calls are fast, and a few are tens of thousands of times slower. With 14 collections in 3 seconds, the obvious suspect is a call that happened to meet a pause, when the garbage collector stops every thread. Fewer allocations mean fewer collections. This step never calls the document store, and while compiling can slow the first calls, it doesn't happen 14 times. On a busy machine some slow calls also wait for a CPU core, which is why you check the GC count, not just the tail.

opening:
Picture the restaurant on a busy Saturday. Most dishes leave the kitchen in minutes, but now and then a table waits half an hour, and nobody can say why. The cooks aren't slow. Then someone notices that every few minutes the whole kitchen stops: the clean plates have run out, and everyone helps wash up. Every step of every dish uses plates, and some steps use far more than they need. The more plates a dish dirties, the more often the kitchen stops.

Most "it's slow, but only sometimes" complaints about a JVM program have that shape. Garbage collection is the washing-up, and the report step from lesson 6 dirtied about 2,400 bytes of objects for every document.

Two easy traps wait here: look at the average, which is fine, and stop, or change three things at once and never learn which one helped. Lesson 6 found the widest boxes. In this lesson, we'll follow a whole evening: measure the slow calls, find the lines that make the garbage, fix one thing at a time and prove each round to the byte. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a kitchen that stops to wash up, and the dishes that wait while it does. The report step dirtied about 2,400 bytes for every document. Two measured rounds later it dirties 56, under its budget, and a test makes sure it stays there.

Now look in your own code for String.format, split( or Pattern.compile( inside a method that runs for every request or every item. Each one takes clean plates on every pass.

Next, we'll meet the slowness that no CPU or allocation profile shows. When threads sit and wait, how does a thread dump tell a stuck thread from a busy one?

sections.h: Start from the symptom: the slowest calls and the GC count, not the average
sections.html:
Here's the code under suspicion, the report step from lesson 6, now in a class called ReportVariants that also holds each round of the fix. It checks the two-letter language with a regex, a small pattern language for matching text. It counts the words with split, and it formats a line for the debug log, which is switched off:

Java
static long slow(Document d) {
    if (!Pattern.compile("^[a-z]{2}$").matcher(d.language()).matches())   // line 17
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language");
    long words = d.text().split(" ").length;                               // line 19
    long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238;
    debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d",     // line 21
            d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds));
    return seconds;
}
Kotlin
fun ktSlow(d: KtDocument): Long {
    require(Regex("^[a-z]{2}$").matches(d.language)) { "bad language" }   // a regex per call
    val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong()                          // a new String per word
    val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238
    ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d"                // formatted, then dropped
        .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds))
    return seconds
}

ReportInvestigation runs it on four threads, four lines of work side by side, for 3 seconds. It does that in a second JVM, with a 256 MB heap (-Xmx256m: the most memory the JVM may use for objects) and a JFR recording, lesson 5's log of what the JVM did. It times every call into a histogram, a fixed array of counters by duration. Then it prints the percentiles. Sort all the calls by time: p50 is the one in the middle, p99 is the one that 99% of calls beat, and only one call in ten thousand is slower than the p99.99. Those rare slow calls are the tail. Here's one run on JDK 25, on the busy course machine:

slow: 218,239 calls/s  p50 <1500ns  p99 <27300ns  p99.9 <110800ns  p99.99 <36700us  GCs 14 (235 ms)

Half the calls take under 1.5 µs. The p99.99 is over 36 ms, more than 20,000 times longer. The JVM collected garbage 14 times in 3 seconds, and jfr view gc-pauses on the same recording agrees: 14 pauses, 236 ms in total, the longest 53.2 ms.

That's our first suspect, and the kitchen explains it. Every object a call creates is a clean plate taken from the shelf. When the young part of the heap, where new objects start out, fills up, the garbage collector stops every thread of the program while it clears the dead objects away: the whole kitchen washing up. A call that's running when a pause starts waits for the pause to end. So the slowest calls are probably the ones that met a pause, and the pauses come often because the code allocates a lot. Here the picture breaks a little. G1, the JVM's default collector, does some of its work while the program runs, like a kitchen porter washing in a corner. But the young collections, the frequent ones here, stop everyone.

One caution before we change anything. This machine shared its four cores with more than 30 busy programs, so some slow calls simply waited for a core, and the p99.9 of 110 µs is probably that. The longest call of a run is mostly that noise too. Don't present it as the effect of a fix. The percentiles and the GC counts are the evidence.

A good median can hide calls that wait for the garbage collector. Measure the tail and count the GCs.

The figure shows the loop this lesson follows. The step people skip is the dashed one. So the GC is the suspect, and allocation is the motive. Which lines allocate?

try.title: Reproduce the symptom
steps: Read ReportVariants.slow and ReportInvestigation. The demo starts a second JVM with -Xmx256m and a JFR recording, runs 4 threads for 3 seconds, then reads the recording.
Predict: which line of slow allocates the most?
Run it with -Pargs=slow. Write down the p50, the p99.99, the GC count and the calls per second.

code.title: ReportInvestigation.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l07; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedEvent; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordedFrame; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile; import java.lang.management.GarbageCollectorMXBean; import java.lang.management.ManagementFactory; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.HashMap; import java.util.List; import java.util.Map; import java.util.function.ToLongFunction; /** * Runs one version of the report step (slow, hoisted, scanned or noregex) on 4 threads for 3 seconds in a * second JVM with -Xmx256m and a JFR recording, prints latency percentiles and GC counts, then reads the * recording and prints allocation by source line in this package. Usage: -Pargs=slow (or hoisted, ...). */ public class ReportInvestigation { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "slow"; if (args.length > 1 && args[1].equals("child")) { load(mode); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "report-" + mode + ".jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:jfr+startup=warning", "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ReportInvestigation.class.getName(), mode, "child") .inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); allocationByLine(file); } // the load: 4 threads, each timing every call into a fixed histogram (no allocation of its own) static void load(String mode) throws Exception { ToLongFunction<ReportVariants.Document> step = switch (mode) { case "slow" -> ReportVariants::slow; case "hoisted" -> ReportVariants::hoisted; case "scanned" -> ReportVariants::scanned; default -> ReportVariants::noRegex; }; ReportVariants.Document[] ds = ReportVariants.documents(4_096); long end = System.nanoTime() + 3_000_000_000L; long[][] hist = new long[4][]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { int id = t; Thread th = new Thread(() -> { long[] h = new long[20_001]; // 100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 us buckets up to 1 s long sink = 0; for (int i = id; System.nanoTime() < end; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); sink += step.applyAsLong(ds[i & 4095]); long d = System.nanoTime() - t0; h[d < 1_000_000 ? (int) (d / 100) : (int) Math.min(20_000, 10_000 + (d - 1_000_000) / 100_000)]++; } hist[id] = h; if (sink == 42) System.out.println(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); long[] h = new long[20_001]; for (long[] x : hist) for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) h[k] += x[k]; long total = 0; for (long n : h) total += n; long gcs = 0, gcMs = 0; for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { gcs += gc.getCollectionCount(); gcMs += gc.getCollectionTime(); } System.out.printf("%s: %,d calls/s p50 %s p99 %s p99.9 %s p99.99 %s GCs %d (%d ms)%n", mode, total / 3, pct(h, total, 0.5), pct(h, total, 0.99), pct(h, total, 0.999), pct(h, total, 0.9999), gcs, gcMs); } static String pct(long[] h, long total, double q) { long target = (long) Math.ceil(total * q), acc = 0; for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) { acc += h[k]; if (acc >= target) return k < 10_000 ? "<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.ReportVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); total += e.getLong("weight"); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } long sum = total; System.out.println("allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from " + file.getFileName() + "):"); weight.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(5) .forEach(en -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * en.getValue() / sum, en.getKey())); } }

in-process JFR recording, then allocation by line in this file. // Usage: -Pargs=slow (or hoisted, scanned, noregex). data class KtDocument(val id: String, val language: String, val text: String) @Volatile var ktDebugEnabled = false fun ktDebug(message: String) { if (ktDebugEnabled) println(message) } // before: a regex per call, a new String per word, a log line formatted and dropped fun require(KT_LANGUAGE.matches(d.language)) { "bad language" } val words = ktCountWords(d.text) val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d".format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } // round 3, if the budget asks for it: no regex for two letters fun isLanguageCodeKt(s: String) = s.length == 2 && s.all { it in 'a'..'z' } fun ktNoRegex(d: KtDocument): Long { require(isLanguageCodeKt(d.language)) { "bad language" } val words = ktCountWords(d.text) val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238 if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d".format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds)) return seconds } private val ktWords = "the rain came early and the river rose over the old stone bridge before noon".split(' ') private val ktLanguages = listOf("en", "fr", "de", "es", "it", "nl") fun ktDocuments(n: Int) = Array(n) { i -> val text = (0 until 8 + i % 7).joinToString(" ") { w -> ktWords[(i * 7 + w * 3) % ktWords.size] } // 8 to 14 words KtDocument("doc-$i", ktLanguages[i % ktLanguages.size], text) } fun main(args: Array<String>) { val mode = args.firstOrNull() ?: "slow" val step: (KtDocument) -> Long = when (mode) { "slow" -> ::ktSlow; "hoisted" -> ::ktHoisted; "scanned" -> ::ktScanned; else -> ::ktNoRegex } val ds = ktDocuments(4_096) val file = Path.of("build", "report-kt-$mode.jfr").toAbsolutePath() val calls = LongArray(4) Recording(Configuration.getConfiguration("profile")).use { rec -> rec.start() val end = System.nanoTime() + 3_000_000_000L (0 until 4).map { t -> thread { var sink = 0L var i = t while (System.nanoTime() < end) { sink += step(ds[i and 4095]); i++; calls[t]++ } if (sink == 42L) println() } }.forEach { it.join() } rec.stop() rec.dump(file) } val gcs = ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans().sumOf { it.collectionCount } println("%s: %,d calls/s, %d GCs".format(mode, calls.sum() / 3, gcs)) val weight = HashMap<String, Long>() for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (e.eventType.name != "jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") continue val frame = e.stackTrace?.frames?.firstOrNull { it.method.type.name == "workbench.performance.l07.ReportInvestigationKt" } ?: continue weight.merge("${frame.method.name} line ${frame.lineNumber}", e.getLong("weight"), Long::plus) } val total = weight.values.sum() println("allocation by line in ReportInvestigation.kt:") weight.entries.sortedByDescending { it.value }.take(5) .forEach { (site, w) -> println(" %5.1f%% %s".format(100.0 * w / total, site)) } }

try.expect: The JVM prints its "Started recording" lines, then one line of numbers and the allocation by line. On the busy course machine, two runs gave 87,194 and 218,239 calls a second, a p50 under 2 µs, a p99.99 of tens of milliseconds and 6 to 14 GCs. The allocation by line puts lines 17, 19 and 21 on top, in an order that changed between runs. The latency numbers move a lot from run to run; the three lines don't.

video.title: The kitchen that stops to wash up: start from the slow tail and the GC count, find the line that allocates, fix one thing at a time

sections.h: JFR names the allocation, and the first frame in your code names the line
sections.html:
jfr view allocation-by-site on the slow run answers "what allocates" in the JDK's words:

Method                                                                 Allocation Pressure
---------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------
java.util.Formatter.parse(String)                                                   16.09%
java.lang.Long.toString(long)                                                       14.19%
java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(String)                                              9.65%
java.util.Arrays.copyOfRange(byte[], int, int)                                       7.79%
java.util.regex.Pattern$BitClass.<init>()                                            7.33%
java.lang.StringLatin1.newString(byte[], int, int)                                   6.83%

That's real, and not yet useful: you can't change Formatter.parse. The view groups by the top frame, the JDK method that did the allocating. What we want is the first frame in our own code below it. Each jdk.ObjectAllocationSample event carries a stack trace and a weight, the number of bytes the sample stands for. So a few lines of RecordingFile, as in lesson 5's lab, can group the samples by our file and line instead:

Java
for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) {
    if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample")) continue;
    for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) {
        if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.ReportVariants")) {
            weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum);
            break;                          // the first frame in our code is the one to change
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
for (e in RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) {
    if (e.eventType.name != "jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") continue
    val frame = e.stackTrace?.frames
        ?.firstOrNull { it.method.type.name == "workbench.performance.l07.ReportInvestigationKt" }
        ?: continue                         // the first frame in our code is the one to change
    weight.merge("${frame.method.name} line ${frame.lineNumber}", e.getLong("weight"), Long::plus)
}

ReportInvestigation does exactly that after each run. For the run above:

allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from report-slow.jfr):
   49.1%  slow line 21      String.format(...) for a log line nobody reads
   32.3%  slow line 17      Pattern.compile(...) on every call
   18.5%  slow line 19      split(" "), a new String for every word

A second run put the same three lines on top in another order: line 17 first with 46.5%, then 19 and 21. JFR samples allocations instead of counting every byte, so read its shares as rough. A big share is big, and the order of near-equals means little. Measured one at a time, with the per-thread counter we'll meet at the end, the regex cost about 800 bytes per call, the log line 810 and split 690, out of 2,460.

A flame graph answers the next question, who calls the allocating code. Lesson 6's allocation profile of the same code put 34.1% of the bytes under String.format, 33.3% under Pattern.compile and 28.2% under split. Two different tools agree, which is the point of using both. JFR is built in and cheap enough to leave running. async-profiler shows the whole picture, native frames included, when you can attach it.

So the three costs have names. The regex is compiled again on every call. split builds a String for every word, only so that we can count them. And a third of all the bytes is a sentence written for the debug log, which is switched off, so nobody ever reads it.

The view names the JDK method that allocated. The first frame in your own code names the line to change.

Three costs, three fixes. The temptation is to make all of them at once.

sections.h: Fix one thing, then profile again
sections.html:
Round 1 removes the two costs that are pure waste, work done for nothing. They're the same kind of fix, so we'll make them together and count them as one round. The pattern becomes a static final field, compiled once, and the log line is formatted only when DEBUG is on. Moving work that doesn't change out of the path that runs on every call is called hoisting.

Java
static final Pattern LANGUAGE = Pattern.compile("^[a-z]{2}$");    // compiled once

static long hoisted(Document d) {
    if (!LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language");   // line 30
    long words = d.text().split(" ").length;                               // line 31
    long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238;
    if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d",   // only when DEBUG is on
            d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds));
    return seconds;
}
Kotlin
val KT_LANGUAGE = Regex("^[a-z]{2}$")                                // compiled once

fun ktHoisted(d: KtDocument): Long {
    require(KT_LANGUAGE.matches(d.language)) { "bad language" }
    val words = d.text.split(' ').size.toLong()
    val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238
    if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d"   // only when DEBUG is on
        .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds))
    return seconds
}

The same harness, on the same busy machine:

hoisted: 767,348 calls/s  p50 <300ns  p99 <4200ns  p99.9 <23500ns  p99.99 <12400us  GCs 15 (161 ms)

Three and a half times the throughput, and the p99.99 down from 36.7 ms to 12.4 ms. But the GC count went up, from 14 to 15. Did the fix fail? No. The faster version made 3.5 times as many calls in the same 3 seconds, so count collections per call: about 21 per million calls before, about 6.5 now.

Then profile again, because the picture has changed:

allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from report-hoisted.jfr):
   91.5%  hoisted line 31      split(" ")
    8.4%  hoisted line 30      LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches()

split was about a quarter of the problem before. Now it's nearly all of it. We already know the cure from lesson 3: count where words start, without building any words. That's round 2:

Java
static long countWords(String text) {          // round 2: count where words start, make nothing
    long words = 0;
    boolean inWord = false;
    for (int i = 0; i < text.length(); i++) {
        boolean letter = text.charAt(i) != ' ';
        if (letter && !inWord) words++;
        inWord = letter;
    }
    return words;
}

static long scanned(Document d) {
    if (!LANGUAGE.matcher(d.language()).matches()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad language");   // line 51
    long words = countWords(d.text());
    long seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238;
    if (debugEnabled) debug(String.format("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d",
            d.id(), d.language(), words, seconds));
    return seconds;
}
Kotlin
fun ktCountWords(text: String): Long {          // round 2: count where words start, make nothing
    var words = 0L
    var inWord = false
    for (c in text) {
        val letter = c != ' '
        if (letter && !inWord) words++
        inWord = letter
    }
    return words
}

fun ktScanned(d: KtDocument): Long {
    require(KT_LANGUAGE.matches(d.language)) { "bad language" }
    val words = ktCountWords(d.text)
    val seconds = (words * 60 + 237) / 238
    if (ktDebugEnabled) ktDebug("document %s language=%s words=%d seconds=%d"
        .format(d.id, d.language, words, seconds))
    return seconds
}

scanned: 2,066,071 calls/s  p50 <200ns  p99 <800ns  p99.9 <6100ns  p99.99 <51200ns  GCs 4 (75 ms)

The p99.99 fell from milliseconds to 51 µs, and the GCs to about 0.65 per million calls. Profile once more, and 99.6% of what's left is on line 51. A precompiled Pattern still creates a new Matcher object, its working state for one match, on every call. That cost was there from the start, a few percent hidden under bigger ones. It only rose to the top once they were gone.

Do we fix it too? The answer depends on a budget: the number of bytes per call you've agreed the step may cost. This one's budget is 300 bytes, and the Matcher costs 56, so round 2 is enough. A third round could check the two letters by hand, and noregex in the demo does: 3.8 million calls a second and no GCs at all. For a two-letter rule, that's a small, safe change. For a rule with ten cases, the regex may be worth its bytes.

Fix one thing, then profile again. The order of costs changes after every fix.

Check yourself: in round 1 you hoist the Pattern but forget to guard the log line. Which line leads the next profile? (Line 21, the String.format: about 810 bytes per call, now the biggest cost left.)

The harness tells us the fix helped. It can't yet tell us by exactly how much.

steps: For each, write down the top line, the p99.99 and the GC count next to your numbers for slow. Work out GCs per million calls, too.

Usage: -Pargs=slow (or hoisted, ...). */ public class ReportInvestigation { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String mode = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "slow"; if (args.length > 1 && args[1].equals("child")) { load(mode); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "report-" + mode + ".jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(java, "-Xmx256m", "-Xlog:jfr+startup=warning", "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), ReportInvestigation.class.getName(), mode, "child") .inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); allocationByLine(file); } // the load: 4 threads, each timing every call into a fixed histogram (no allocation of its own) static void load(String mode) throws Exception { ToLongFunction<ReportVariants.Document> step = switch (mode) { case "slow" -> ReportVariants::slow; case "hoisted" -> ReportVariants::hoisted; case "scanned" -> ReportVariants::scanned; default -> ReportVariants::noRegex; }; ReportVariants.Document[] ds = ReportVariants.documents(4_096); long end = System.nanoTime() + 3_000_000_000L; long[][] hist = new long[4][]; List<Thread> threads = new ArrayList<>(); for (int t = 0; t < 4; t++) { int id = t; Thread th = new Thread(() -> { long[] h = new long[20_001]; // 100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 us buckets up to 1 s long sink = 0; for (int i = id; System.nanoTime() < end; i++) { long t0 = System.nanoTime(); sink += step.applyAsLong(ds[i & 4095]); long d = System.nanoTime() - t0; h[d < 1_000_000 ? (int) (d / 100) : (int) Math.min(20_000, 10_000 + (d - 1_000_000) / 100_000)]++; } hist[id] = h; if (sink == 42) System.out.println(); }); th.start(); threads.add(th); } for (Thread th : threads) th.join(); long[] h = new long[20_001]; for (long[] x : hist) for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) h[k] += x[k]; long total = 0; for (long n : h) total += n; long gcs = 0, gcMs = 0; for (GarbageCollectorMXBean gc : ManagementFactory.getGarbageCollectorMXBeans()) { gcs += gc.getCollectionCount(); gcMs += gc.getCollectionTime(); } System.out.printf("%s: %,d calls/s p50 %s p99 %s p99.9 %s p99.99 %s GCs %d (%d ms)%n", mode, total / 3, pct(h, total, 0.5), pct(h, total, 0.99), pct(h, total, 0.999), pct(h, total, 0.9999), gcs, gcMs); } static String pct(long[] h, long total, double q) { long target = (long) Math.ceil(total * q), acc = 0; for (int k = 0; k < h.length; k++) { acc += h[k]; if (acc >= target) return k < 10_000 ? "<" + (k + 1) * 100 + "ns" : "<" + ((k - 10_000 + 1) * 100 + 1_000) + "us"; } return "?"; } // what `jfr view allocation-by-site` can't tell you: the line in YOUR code each sample came from static void allocationByLine(Path file) throws Exception { Map<String, Long> weight = new HashMap<>(); long total = 0; for (RecordedEvent e : RecordingFile.readAllEvents(file)) { if (!e.getEventType().getName().equals("jdk.ObjectAllocationSample") || e.getStackTrace() == null) continue; for (RecordedFrame f : e.getStackTrace().getFrames()) { if (f.getMethod().getType().getName().startsWith("workbench.performance.l07.ReportVariants")) { weight.merge(f.getMethod().getName() + " line " + f.getLineNumber(), e.getLong("weight"), Long::sum); total += e.getLong("weight"); break; // the first frame in our code is the one to change } } } long sum = total; System.out.println("allocation by line in ReportVariants.java (from " + file.getFileName() + "):"); weight.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed()).limit(5) .forEach(en -> System.out.printf(" %5.1f%% %s%n", 100.0 * en.getValue() / sum, en.getKey())); } }

try.expect: hoisted puts about 90% of the remaining allocation on line 31 (split) and the rest on line 30 (the Matcher). scanned puts almost all of it on line 51, the Matcher. noregex shows only a few samples from the demo's own set-up (documents) and no GCs. Throughput goes up several times and the p99.99 drops to tens of microseconds, although the exact numbers vary a lot on a busy machine. The Kotlin twin's scanned run leaves almost everything (97.1% in one run) in ktScanned, where the only thing that allocates is the Matcher behind KT_LANGUAGE.matches(...): Kotlin's Regex makes one too.

sections.h: Prove it with JMH, then keep it with an allocation budget
sections.html:
JMH, the OpenJDK benchmark tool from lesson 3, gives the exact answer, with -prof gc and its bytes per operation. ReportBench runs each round on one document of 12 words (one fork, 5 warm-up and 3 measured rounds of 0.3 s each):

Benchmark           ns/op      error         B/op    error
after1Hoisted       856.5     7035.0      832.020    0.165
after2Scanned       311.6     2163.9       56.007    0.047
after3NoRegex       136.9      424.4        0.003    0.010
before             1776.1     6654.6     2464.040    0.128

The time column says the fixes helped, with errors bigger than the scores on this machine. The bytes column says how much, to a fraction of a byte: 2,464, then 832, then 56, then nothing. One run earlier, before showed 2499.551 ± 907.021 instead. On a machine this busy, five short warm-up rounds weren't always enough for the JIT to finish compiling the regex code, so one measured round still ran slower code that allocated more. Once the code is warm, bytes don't wobble. Before it's warm, they can.

A benchmark proves the fix today. A test keeps it fixed. The JVM counts the bytes each thread allocates, and com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() reads that counter:

Java
var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes();
for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) sink += report.readingSeconds(ds[i & 1023]);
double perCall = (threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before) / 100_000.0;
assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(300);          // the budget
Kotlin
val threads = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean() as com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean
val before = threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes
repeat(100_000) { sink += report.readingSeconds(ds[it and 1023]) }
val perCall = (threads.currentThreadAllocatedBytes - before) / 100_000.0
assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(300.0)         // the budget

That's an allocation budget test: it fails the build when the code allocates more than the agreed bytes per call, which is the check lesson 3 promised. Measure after warm-up, because allocation only settles once C2 has compiled the method and its escape analysis, the trick of skipping objects that never leave a method, has done its work. The lab's test runs 10 rounds of 100,000 calls and judges the best one. Measured that way, the slow version settles at about 2,400 bytes per call. Round 1 settles at about 750 on JDK 25 and 820 on JDK 21, and round 2 at 56 on JDK 25 and 128 on JDK 21. The numbers move with the JDK and with the shape of the loop, so set the budget with a margin, and look at it again when you upgrade.

Here's where this loop stops. It finds code that burns CPU or makes garbage. Some programs are slow, or frozen, because their threads are waiting for each other, or for something outside the JVM. A profile of a waiting thread shows almost nothing, so that needs a different look.

Bytes per call is the number to keep. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 300, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class ReportBench { ReportVariants.Document doc = new ReportVariants.Document("doc-7", "fr", "the rain came early and the river rose over the old stone"); // non-final input @Benchmark public long before() { return ReportVariants.slow(doc); } @Benchmark public long after1Hoisted() { return ReportVariants.hoisted(doc); } @Benchmark public long after2Scanned() { return ReportVariants.scanned(doc); } @Benchmark public long after3NoRegex() { return ReportVariants.noRegex(doc); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var options = new OptionsBuilder() .include(ReportBench.class.getName()) .addProfiler(GCProfiler.class) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build(); System.out.printf("%-14s %10s %10s %12s %8s%n", "Benchmark", "ns/op", "error", "B/op", "error"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var time = r.getPrimaryResult(); var bytes = r.getSecondaryResults().get("gc.alloc.rate.norm"); System.out.printf("%-14s %10.1f %10.1f %12.3f %8.3f%n", r.getParams().getBenchmark().replaceAll(".*\\.", ""), time.getScore(), time.getScoreError(), bytes.getScore(), bytes.getScoreError()); } } }

compare.note: After round 2 both versions allocate 56 bytes per call on JDK 25, all of it the Matcher behind the language check: Kotlin's Regex.matches creates one, just like Pattern.matcher. Round 1 cost 832 bytes in Java and 840 in Kotlin, where split(' ') returns a List<String> instead of an array. One Kotlin detail is worth knowing. The harness calls each version through a function type, (KtDocument) -> Long, whose invoke returns an object, so every result is boxed into a Long. Here that costs nothing, because Long.valueOf keeps ready-made objects for -128 to 127 and reading times are small. A function returning bigger numbers would allocate on every call. In hot Kotlin code, call the function directly, pass it to an inline function, or use a fun interface with a primitive return type, the Kotlin counterpart of Java's ToLongFunction.

worked.title: Write up the investigation for the pull request

steps.say: A pull request is the proposed change that reviewers read before it's merged. Start with the symptom and how you measured it, with the conditions. Without the conditions, the numbers mean nothing to a reviewer.
steps.code:
Symptom: report step p99.99 < 36.7 ms (p50 < 1.5 us); 14 GCs in 3 s.
Setup: 4 threads, 3 s, -Xmx256m, JDK 25, 4 shared cores, a latency histogram per call.

steps.say: Then the evidence for the cause, from two tools, with the lines named.
steps.code:
JFR jdk.ObjectAllocationSample, first frame in our code (two runs):
  line 21 String.format for a disabled DEBUG line  49.1% / 24.4%
  line 17 Pattern.compile on every call            32.3% / 46.5%
  line 19 split(" "), a String per word             18.5% / 28.8%
async-profiler alloc: format 34.1%, Pattern.compile 33.3%, split 28.2% of bytes

steps.say: Then each round on its own, with the profile that justified the next one. Self-check: why list round 1, even though round 2 includes it? (So the reviewer sees what each change bought, and that the next cost was found by measuring, not guessed.)
steps.code:
Round 1 (hoist the pattern, guard the log line): p99.99 < 12.4 ms, 6.5 GCs per million calls.
  Profile again: 91.5% of allocation now at split(" ").
Round 2 (count words without split): p99.99 < 51.2 us, 0.65 GCs per million calls.
  Profile again: 99.6% at LANGUAGE.matcher(...). 56 B/call, under the 300 B budget. Stopping.

steps.say: End with the proof and the guard: the JMH numbers with their errors, and the test that keeps it fixed.
steps.code:
JMH -prof gc (1 fork, 5 warm-up + 3 x 0.3 s): before 2,464.040 +/- 0.128 B/op, after 56.007 +/- 0.047 B/op.
DocumentReportTest.allocationBudget: < 300 B/call after warm-up (JDK 25: 56, JDK 21: 128).

lab.title: Bring the report step under its allocation budget
steps: Open DocumentReport. Its readingSeconds checks the language, counts the words, works out the reading time and writes a DEBUG line through DebugLog, a tiny logging interface. Run the tests. Three pass (reading times, language check, DEBUG message) and one fails: the slow version settles at about 2,400 bytes per call, against a budget of 300.
Optional but worth it: run ReportInvestigation -Pargs=slow and read the allocation by line. DocumentReport has the same three costs.

Round 1: make the pattern a static final field, and format the DEBUG line only when log.isDebugEnabled(). Run the tests. The budget test still fails, now at about 750 bytes (820 on JDK 21). Its failure message lists every round it measured.
Round 2: count the words without split, by walking the characters and counting where words start, as in lesson 3. Run the tests until all four pass.
Keep the reading times, the bad language message and the exact DEBUG text: the other three tests guard them. Optional round 3: replace the regex with a check for exactly two letters from a to z.
hints: Pattern.compile(...) in a static final field stops the compile, but matcher() still creates a Matcher on every call. That's what's left after round 2: 56 bytes on JDK 25, 128 on JDK 21, both under the budget.
The budget test measures 10 rounds of 100,000 calls and judges the best one, so a slow start while the JIT warms up won't fail it.

For the words: keep a boolean inWord. A character that isn't a space, after a space or at the start, begins a new word. The texts have single spaces and at least one word, so this count equals split(" ").length.
The DEBUG text must stay exactly document doc-7 language=fr words=12 seconds=4. Keep the String.format call and only move it inside the if.

drill.prompt: Close this page. Write down, in order, the steps you take from "the report step's p99.99 is bad" to a merged fix, naming the tool and the exact number you look at in each step. Then write the core of an allocation budget test.

JMH -prof gc: gc.alloc.rate.norm (B/op) before and after, with its error // 6. allocation budget test, with a margin, looked at again on JDK upgrades var threads = (com.sun.management.ThreadMXBean) ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean(); for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) sink += report.readingSeconds(ds[i & 1023]); // warm up first long before = threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes(); for (int i = 0; i < 100_000; i++) sink += report.readingSeconds(ds[i & 1023]); double perCall = (threads.getCurrentThreadAllocatedBytes() - before) / 100_000.0; assertThat(perCall).isLessThan(300);

recap: Start from the tail (p99.9, p99.99) and the GC count. A good median can hide calls that waited for a GC pause; on a busy machine some waited for a CPU core, and the longest call is mostly noise.

JFR's allocation-by-site names JDK methods; group the samples by the first frame in your own code and its line to find what to change. JFR samples, so treat its shares as rough, and let a flame graph confirm the callers.

Fix one thing at a time and profile again: split filled 92% of the profile after round 1, and the Matcher 99.6% after round 2. Count GCs per call, not per second, because a faster version makes more calls.
Stop when what's left fits the budget or is the work itself: here 56 bytes of Matcher against a budget of 300.

Prove it with JMH -prof gc (2,464 to 56 B/op, errors under a byte once warm) and keep it with an allocation budget test with a margin, because the numbers move between JDKs and loops (56 on JDK 25, 128 on JDK 21).
The limit: this loop finds code that burns CPU or makes garbage. Threads that wait for each other, or for something outside the JVM, barely show in it (lesson 8).

explain.prompt: Explain to a new teammate how you'd investigate "the report step's p99.99 is bad", from the first measurement to the merged fix, and why each step is there.
explain.answer: First I'd measure the tail properly: percentiles and the GC count under a realistic load, because the median can look perfect while one call in ten thousand waits for a GC pause. If the GC is busy, I take a JFR recording and look at gc-pauses and at allocation, grouped by the first frame in our own code, so I get a file and a line instead of JDK internals. A flame graph confirms who calls the allocating code. Then I fix one thing, the biggest waste, and measure again, because the order changes and new hot spots appear, like split after the regex and the log line, and then the Matcher. I stop when what's left fits the budget. Before merging, I prove the change with a JMH benchmark using -prof gc, since bytes per operation are steady and time isn't, and I add an allocation budget test with some margin, so a later change can't bring the cost back unnoticed.

deeper.html:
The harness in this lesson measured latency without adding garbage of its own. Its histogram is a fixed array of counters (100 ns buckets up to 1 ms, then 100 µs buckets up to 1 s), filled in place. A latency recorder that allocated an object per call would add exactly the garbage you're trying to measure. HdrHistogram is the usual library for this in real services.

Measuring still costs something. Lesson 6's CPU profile showed 64 of 3,569 samples in reading the clock, because the demo calls System.nanoTime() on every lap, and this harness calls it twice per call. On an operation of a few hundred nanoseconds, that's a real share. It's one more reason the final proof is a JMH benchmark rather than the load harness.

Many logging libraries take a message pattern and its arguments separately, for example log.debug("document {} words={}", id, words) in SLF4J, a common logging library, and build the text only when the level is on. That removes the formatting, but the arguments are still computed, numbers are still boxed, and a call with many arguments still builds an array for them. In a hot path, the explicit if (log.isDebugEnabled()) guard is the version you can reason about. A profile will tell you if it matters.

The cost of split grows with every word, while the scan's stays at zero. The documents here have 8 to 14 words. Lesson 3 counted 544 bytes per line of nine words, so a 2,000-word chapter split this way would make about 120 KB of short strings, just to be counted.
